title: Hello, World!
description: Write your first Python program and learn how print() works.

blocks.content:
## Your First Python Program

The simplest program you can write just displays a message:

```python
print("Hello, World!")
```

Run it and you get:
```
Hello, World!
```

`print()` is a built-in function that displays whatever you put inside the parentheses. The text goes inside quotes - either single `'` or double `"`, they work the same.

You can print multiple things by separating them with commas:

```python
print("Hello", "World")
# Hello World

print("Score:", 42)
# Score: 42
```

`print()` tells Python to show something on the screen. It is your easiest way to check that a program is doing what you think it is doing.

Words need quotation marks because Python must know they are text, not a variable name it should look up.

blocks.question:
What does this code print?

```python
print("2 + 3")
```
blocks.explanation: The quotes make `2 + 3` a string (text). Python prints it exactly as written. Without quotes - `print(2 + 3)` - Python would do the math first and print `5`.

blocks.content:
## Comments

A comment is a note in your code that Python ignores. It's there for you (or other people reading the code) to understand what's going on.

Start a comment with `#`. Everything after `#` on that line is ignored:

```python
# This line is a comment - Python skips it
print("Hello!")  # This part is also a comment
```

Use comments to:
- Explain what a piece of code does
- Leave a note for your future self
- Temporarily disable a line while testing

blocks.question: What happens when Python reaches a line that starts with `#`?
options: It prints the line to the screen
It saves the line to a file
blocks.explanation: Lines starting with `#` are comments. Python skips them completely - they have no effect on how the program runs. Comments only exist to help people reading the code.
